Rachel · Genesis 30:22

Husbands are Terrible gods

From The God Who Hears Her by Dr. Connie Champeon · 2 min read

“She [Leah] said, “This time I will praise the LORD.” Therefore she named him Judah. Then she stopped bearing.

“When Rachel saw that she bore Jacob no children, Rachel envied her sister. She said to Jacob, “Give me children, or else I will die.” Jacob’s anger burned against Rachel, and he said, “Am I in God’s place, who has withheld from you the fruit of the womb?” She said, “Behold, my maid Bilhah. Go in to her, that she may bear on my knees, and I also may obtain children by her.”” (Genesis 29:35-30:3)

“God remembered Rachel, and God listened to her, and opened her womb.” (Genesis 30:22)

These verses are jarring if the numbers don’t interrupt your reading between chapter 29 and 30. (Can you tell that I really hate chapter and verse numbers?!) The first hearers received this as one continuous account, read aloud. Chapter numbers and headings break it into pieces they never had. If you’ve never had the joy of reading a Bible that doesn’t have them, I’d strongly encourage it. Such Bibles are uncommon, but reading one will change how you read and understand the Word. But I digress. In this section, we move on from Leah’s striving to her celebration of the enoughness of God, and then we are confronted with Rachel demanding that Jacob be God. Finally, at the end of all the striving, God does for Rachel what Jacob never could: He remembers her, He listens to her, and He opens her womb.

Jacob is still acting like a young man rather than a man of eighty. Jacob resents Rachel’s expectations. If it’s acceptable for society to treat you like a god, you shouldn’t get upset when people expect you to produce results like one. I have seen this on more than one occasion from leaders. Even if people’s expectations are unreasonable, a leader’s responding in anger pushes people deeper into despair. It is humbling for a leader to say, “I can’t do that or fix things, but I can take you to the One who can.” When I respond with intercession, like Isaac did for Rebekah in Genesis 25:21, I lead them to the Source. Anger, frustration, exhaustion, trying to do it all myself are responses that make the story about me and lean towards narcissism. Confessing that I am not enough is good for my soul, it is like deeply inhaling God’s grace. When we go together to the only One who is enough, we can find rest in His greatness. Jesus never got angry when people were desperate; instead, He always countered with grace. He often responded with “Your faith has made you well,” making it about them and God.

Although Jacob pushes Rachel deeper into despair and into a choice that was unwise (maybe Jacob never told her about Sarah and Hagar!), once again God hears His daughters. How often ezers, carrying Eve's brokenness, look to men for all the things only God can give. We were designed to strengthen and assist in battle, not plead with men for favors or look to to give us what we need. Only God is adequate to respond to those needs for us. Only God can provide what we lack and fill the emptiness in our hearts. “Bone of my bone and flesh of my flesh,” is how Adam greeted Eve, but it is not only a husband's words. Laban says it to Jacob a few verses before this passage. The tribes of Israel say it to David. It is the language of belonging. Every one of us — married, single, or widowed — was made to stand alongside God's people and show His image together with them.

Who or what am I looking to today to provide the things only God can provide? What bad choices am I making because I’m trying to fix situations myself or looking to others instead of Him?
